metadata.file_name: Euro J of Education - 2025 - Bozkuş - Predictors of Reading Performance of Fourth‐Graders.pdf
metadata.title: Predictors of Reading Performance of Fourth-­Graders

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading data and acknowledges the PIRLS complex sampling design, including plausible values, weights, and stratification. For the student reading scores, the authors select the first plausible value ASRIBM01 as the representative reading benchmark, but they explicitly state that weights and sampling strata were not directly incorporated into the machine learning analysis. This means the SVM classification and SVM-RFE feature selection were run without applying PIRLS sampling weights (and without replicate-weight variance estimation). The analytic sample was created by deleting cases/variables with more than 20% missing data, imputing remaining missing values using k-nearest-neighbour mean imputation (k=10), and then normalising the predictors via centering and variance scaling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data were extracted from the public PIRLS 2021 dataset (student, teacher, home, and school questionnaires merged into one file). The raw merged file contained 413,387 students; samples with more than 20% missing data were deleted, reducing the dataset to 289,911. Remaining missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbour mean imputation with k=10, and predictors were normalised (centering and variance scaling). The dependent variable was constructed by recoding the PIRLS benchmark reading score ASRIBM01 (first plausible value) into a binary identifier: low performance = first two benchmark categories (<475) and high performance = last two categories (>=550), yielding an analytic dataset of 204,176 students with 122 independent variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading (ASRIBM01 first plausible value; binary high vs low)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (L2-regularised, linear kernel) with 3x repeated 10-fold CV: Accuracy 84.3% (95% CI 0.841–0.846, p<2.2e−16), sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.88. Hold-out split: train 70% (n=142,924) / test 30% (n=61,252). Confusion matrix on test predictions: 22,717 true negatives, 28,951 true positives, 3,967 false positives, 5,617 false negatives (total 51,252 predictions). RFE subset-size performance (RMSE/R2/MAE): 4 vars (0.4618/0.1417/0.4287), 8 vars (0.4088/0.3275/0.3471), 16 vars (0.3864/0.3992/0.3197), 122 vars (0.3544/0.4946/0.2867).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged home internet access, home study desk/table, school library availability, ineffective classroom rules, and number of books at home to predict reading performance group (high vs low), finding that the SVM achieved 84.3% accuracy with sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.88. This indicates that family-level resources and home learning conditions (especially digital access and study space) are the most actionable correlates for identifying low-performing readers, though the model is trained on a binary recode of a single plausible value and does not incorporate PIRLS sampling weights.

data.outcome_summary: This study used PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading data (ASRIBM01, the first plausible value) and recoded the benchmark reading score into a binary outcome: low performance (<475) versus high performance (≥550). The authors trained an L2-regularised linear-kernel SVM and evaluated it with 3-times repeated 10-fold cross-validation, reporting 84.3% accuracy (95% CI 0.841–0.846), sensitivity 0.80, and specificity 0.88; on the test set (n=61,252) the confusion matrix showed 22,717 true negatives and 28,951 true positives. Using SVM-RFE, they ranked 122 contextual variables and found that the top 16 factors captured much of the predictive performance (RMSE/R2/MAE improved from 4 to 16 variables and further with all 122). The most influential predictors were largely family-level socioeconomic and home learning resources (internet, study desk/room, books, smartphone), alongside student motivation/reading self-perceptions and school factors (library, absenteeism, classroom rule effectiveness). A key limitation is that plausible values were reduced to a single PV and PIRLS sampling weights/strata were not incorporated into the ML analysis.
